summary: Vichada stands under the national framework of Colombia, and no region-specific signal was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment carried by the parent record applies.
tangentialFactors:
The documented pattern of territorial violence by armed actors comes from other Colombian departments, not Vichada. In Caquetá, the Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign, distributing flyers and WhatsApp messages naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman standing as a local election candidate was given one week by three armed men to leave town and fled at night after hiding, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed.

National totals in this material are raw counts with no per-capita denominator: 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, eight trans women killed between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023. These figures are national, are not attributable to Vichada, and any ranking of departments by raw incident counts would track population size rather than comparative danger.

The killing of Sara Millerey in Bello, Antioquia, attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025 and filmed, with the video circulating on 5 April and her death from cardiac arrest that afternoon, drew an urgent investigation ordered by the president; police questioned local residents and, as of 14 April 2025, no one had been arrested. The bearing for Vichada is that the national record shows trans people killed in daylight and on camera without arrest following.
localsOnly: No resident-facing facts specific to Vichada were sourced: the inventory contains no material on local enforcement of identification rules, local institutions, or the position of trans residents in the department.
outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved and not sourced: whether armed-group threat campaigns of the kind documented in Caquetá and Guajira operate in Vichada, whether any trans person has been killed or displaced in the department, and how local police and notaries apply the national identification and premises-access rules. The two sources in this inventory concern Antioquia and Caquetá, so Vichada's own enforcement environment, facilities access and violence record remain unverified.
